lessons.title: Lesson 1: Choosing your business path
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Compare business paths and choose the one that fits your goals and situation.
This lesson builds toward: Given your money, hours, skills and limits, you will compare two or three business paths and choose the one that fits, writing at least one reason for your choice.
There is more than one road to owning a business. A side hustle earns extra money with little setup. A small service business (cleaning, lawn care, hauling) grows with customers and crews. A product business (food, crafts, clothing) needs supplies and selling space. An online business sells through a website or marketplace. Some people buy into a franchise or join with others in a cooperative.
Match the path to your life: how much money you can risk, how many hours you have, your skills, transportation, any licensing rules, and for people on supervision, your parole or probation conditions.
Ask AI to compare: "I have $500, 20 hours a week, cooking skills and no car. Compare a meal-prep business, catering help and selling baked goods at markets: startup cost, time to first sale, licenses to check and risks." Then verify the license and cost parts with official sources.
Step by step:
- List your money, hours, skills and limits.
- List two or three business ideas.
- Ask AI to compare startup cost, time to first sale, licenses and risks.
- Verify licenses and costs with official sources.
- Pick one path to plan.
Words to know:
- Entrepreneur: a person who starts and runs a business.
- Franchise: a business you buy into that uses another company's brand and system.
- Cooperative: a business owned and run by its members.
Try it now: Write your money, hours, skills and limits. Ask AI to compare two or three ideas, then choose one path and write why.
You can now compare business paths and choose one that fits your life.

options: A business owned by its members
A business you buy into that uses another company's brand and system
check.why: A franchise uses another company's brand and system for a fee.

check.q: You have little money and evenings free. AI suggests opening a restaurant. What would you do?
options: Open the restaurant because AI said so
Compare it with lower-cost paths that fit your money and hours
Borrow as much as you can
check.why: Choose the path that fits your real money, time and skills.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Building a lean business plan with AI
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Write a one-page lean business plan covering all nine parts.
This lesson builds toward: With AI interviewing you, you will write a one-page lean business plan that covers all nine parts, with every guessed number marked to check.
The SBA describes two kinds of business plans: a long traditional plan that lenders often ask for, and a lean startup plan that fits on one page. Start lean.
The SBA's lean plan has nine parts: key partnerships, key activities, key resources, value proposition (why customers choose you), customer relationships, customer segments (who your customers are), channels (how you reach them), cost structure and revenue streams.
Ask AI to help: "Help me fill out a lean business plan with these nine parts for my mobile car detailing business in [city]. Ask me questions one at a time." Answer with real facts. Then check AI's cost guesses against real prices you look up.
Step by step:
- Open a one-page template with nine boxes.
- Ask AI to interview you one question at a time for each part.
- Fill in each box with real facts.
- Check costs and prices against real quotes.
- Keep it to one page.
Words to know:
- Lean business plan: a one-page plan covering the key parts of a business.
- Value proposition: why customers should choose you.
- Revenue stream: a way the business earns money.
Official sources:
- SBA: Write your business plan
Try it now: Fill out a one-page lean plan for your chosen business with AI interviewing you. Mark any part where you need to look up real numbers.
You can now write a one-page lean business plan with AI help.

check.q: What does "revenue streams" mean in a lean plan?
check.why: Revenue streams are the ways money comes in.

check.q: AI fills in your monthly rent cost with a guess. What would you do?
options: Leave it; AI is usually right
Double the number to be safe
Mark it and look up the real price
check.why: Guessed numbers must be checked against real prices.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Testing the idea with real customers
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Talk to ten possible customers and use what they say to improve the plan.
This lesson builds toward: With a list of three customer questions, you will interview possible customers and use what they say to change your plan, talking to at least ten people and changing at least one part of the plan.
A plan is a guess until customers prove it. Talk to at least ten people who match your customer segment. Ask about their problem, not your idea: "How do you get your car cleaned now? What do you pay? What annoys you about it?"
Then test buying: offer a pre-order, a starter price or a sign-up list. People saying "great idea" is nice; people paying or signing up is proof.
Paste your notes (no names or phone numbers) into AI and ask: "Summarize what these ten customers said. What patterns do you see, and what should I change in my plan?" Update the lean plan with what you learned.
Step by step:
- Write three questions about the customer's problem.
- Talk to at least ten possible customers.
- Offer a pre-order, starter price or sign-up list.
- Ask AI to find patterns in your notes, with names removed.
- Update the lean plan.
Words to know:
- Customer segment: a group of customers with similar needs.
- Validate: prove with real evidence that customers want something.
- Pre-order: a customer agrees to buy before the product or service is ready.
Try it now: Talk to at least five possible customers this week using your three questions. Have AI summarize the patterns and change one part of your lean plan.
You can now test a business idea with real customers and improve the plan.

check.q: What is the best question for a customer interview?
options: "How do you handle this problem now?"
check.why: Asking about their problem and what they do now gives honest evidence.

check.q: Eight of ten people say they would never pay for your service. What would you do?
options: Ask AI to say they are wrong
Change the plan, such as the price, the service or the customer
check.why: Customer evidence is meant to change the plan before you spend money.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Setting up, funding and launching

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Business structure, registration and tax ID basics
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: List the setup steps your business needs and the official places to check them.
This lesson builds toward: For your business, you will list the structure, name registration, licenses, permits and tax ID steps, with the official website for each, with every step linked to an official source.
Common U.S. business structures: a sole proprietorship (you and the business are the same; simplest), an LLC (limited liability company; can separate business debts from personal ones, with state fees and paperwork), and corporations. Nonprofits are a separate path. Ask AI to explain the differences, then choose with help from a free business counselor or professional.
Setup often includes: registering a business name with your state or county, getting city or county business licenses, special permits (food, childcare, trucking, cosmetology and others), and a tax ID. The IRS says an Employer Identification Number (EIN) is free when you apply with the IRS; beware of websites that charge for it.
Rules and fees differ by state and city, so make a checklist and confirm each item on official sites: your Secretary of State, your city or county, your state tax agency and irs.gov. Some licenses consider criminal records; the licensing agency explains its rules.
Step by step:
- Ask AI to explain sole proprietorship vs LLC for your situation.
- Confirm your choice with a free counselor or professional.
- List name registration, licenses and permits to check.
- Find each on official state, county and city sites.
- Apply for an EIN for free at irs.gov if you need one.
Words to know:
- Sole proprietorship: a business owned by one person with no separate legal entity.
- LLC: limited liability company: a business structure that can separate business and personal debts.
- Secretary of State: the state office that often handles business registrations.
Official sources:
- IRS: Get an Employer Identification Number
- SBA: Choose a business structure
Try it now: Make a setup checklist for your business: structure, name registration, licenses, permits and EIN. Next to each, write the official website where you will confirm it.
You can now list the setup steps a business needs and where to confirm each one.

options: A business license from the city
A tax ID number for a business from the IRS
check.why: An EIN is the IRS tax ID number for a business.

check.q: A friend says you do not need a permit for a home food business. What would you do?
options: Check with your city, county or state health office
Ask AI and trust its answer
Start selling and wait to see
check.why: Permit rules differ by place, so confirm with the official office.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Funding your start and finding free help
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Build a realistic funding plan and a list of free help, and avoid funding scams.
This lesson builds toward: Given your startup costs, you will build a funding plan and a free-help list, and spot funding scams, with at least three real options and no up-front-fee offers.
Most small businesses start with personal savings, early sales and help from family or community. Start as small as you can and grow with sales. Ask AI to help you list startup costs and find ways to cut them, such as renting equipment or using a shared kitchen.
If you need a loan, look at mission lenders. The SBA's microloan program provides loans up to $50,000 through nonprofit, community-based lenders; the SBA says the average is about $13,000 and the longest term is seven years. Community development financial institutions (CDFIs) and local loan funds also serve people banks often turn away. Grants exist but are usually competitive and specific.
Free help: the SBA points to Small Business Development Centers, SCORE mentors, Women's Business Centers and Veterans Business Outreach Centers for free or low-cost counseling. Beware of anyone who promises guaranteed grants or loans for an upfront fee: that is a common scam.
Step by step:
- List startup costs and cut where you can.
- Plan to start small and grow with sales.
- Look up SBA microloan lenders and CDFIs near you.
- Find your nearest SBDC, SCORE or other SBA partner.
- Never pay upfront fees for "guaranteed" grants or loans.
Words to know:
- Microloan: a small business loan, often from a community lender.
- CDFI: community development financial institution: a lender focused on underserved communities.
- Grant: money you do not pay back, usually given for a specific purpose.
Official sources:
- SBA: Microloans
- SBA: Local assistance
Try it now: List your startup costs and cut at least one. Then find two real funding options and one free counseling center near you (or online) and write how to contact them.
You can now make a realistic funding plan, find free help and spot funding scams.

options: A lender focused on underserved communities
check.why: CDFIs are lenders that focus on underserved communities.

check.q: An online ad promises a guaranteed grant if you pay a fee first. What would you do?
options: Pay the fee quickly before it is gone
Send your bank details to check
Treat it as a likely scam and do not pay
check.why: Real grants do not ask for an up-front fee to guarantee money.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Building your 90-day launch roadmap
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Turn your plan into a 90-day launch roadmap with dates.
This lesson builds toward: Using your plan and checklist, you will create a 90-day launch roadmap with dates for setup, testing and launch, with a date for every step and an accountability partner named.
A roadmap turns the plan into action. Split 90 days into three parts. Days 1-30: set up (structure, registrations, licenses, bank account, basic tools). Days 31-60: prepare and pre-sell (supplies, pricing, marketing, first customers lined up). Days 61-90: launch and learn (first sales, customer feedback, money tracking, adjust).
Ask AI: "Turn my lean plan and setup checklist into a 90-day launch roadmap table with week, task and done-by date. I have 20 hours a week." Then make it real: move dates to fit your life and add buffer time for slow government offices.
Pick one weekly check-in time to review the roadmap, and share it with someone who will hold you accountable, like a mentor, counselor or friend. Celebrate the first sale.
Step by step:
- Days 1-30: setup tasks.
- Days 31-60: prepare and pre-sell.
- Days 61-90: launch, track money and learn.
- Ask AI to draft the table, then adjust the dates.
- Set a weekly check-in and an accountability partner.
Words to know:
- Roadmap: a plan that shows steps in order with dates.
- Accountability partner: someone who checks on your progress and encourages you.
Try it now: Final task: build your 90-day launch roadmap with AI and adjust it. Add it to your lean plan, customer notes, setup checklist and funding and help list to complete your business launch packet.
You can now turn a business idea into a launch-ready plan and a 90-day roadmap.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Lean business plan Parts are missing, or guessed numbers are treated as facts. One page covering all nine parts, with guessed numbers marked or checked. Real prices are filled in and the plan reflects customer feedback. Customer evidence Fewer than ten conversations, or no change to the plan. Notes from at least ten conversations and at least one change to the plan. Has stronger proof such as pre-orders or sign-ups. Setup checklist Steps are missing or have no official source. Structure, registrations, licenses, permits and EIN listed, each with an official website. Notes which steps cost money and which office to call with questions. Funding and free help Fewer than three real options, or includes an up-front-fee offer. At least three real funding or free-help options with how to contact them. Startup costs are cut and an appointment with a counselor is booked. 90-day roadmap No dates, or steps are out of order. Setup, testing and launch steps with a date for each. Names an accountability partner and weekly check-ins. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: What is the focus of days 31 to 60 in a 90-day roadmap?
options: Testing with first customers and improving
check.why: The middle month is for testing and improving before full launch.

check.q: You keep missing roadmap dates. What would you do?
options: Ask an accountability partner to check your progress each week
check.why: An accountability partner helps you keep going and adjust the plan.
